verses.text: A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.
The tongue of the wise commends knowledge, but the mouth of the fool spouts folly.
The eyes of the LORD are in every place, observing the evil and the good.
A soothing tongue is a tree of life, but a perverse tongue crushes the spirit.
A fool rejects his father's discipline, but whoever heeds correction is prudent.
The house of the righteous has great treasure, but the income of the wicked is trouble.
The lips of the wise spread knowledge, but not so the hearts of fools.
The sacrifice of the wicked is detestable to the LORD, but the prayer of the upright is His delight.
The LORD detests the way of the wicked, but He loves those who pursue righteousness.
Discipline is harsh for him who leaves the path; he who hates correction will die.
Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the LORD— how much more the hearts of men!
A mocker does not love to be reproved, nor will he consult the wise.
A joyful heart makes a cheerful countenance, but sorrow of the heart crushes the spirit.
A discerning heart seeks knowledge, but the mouth of a fool feeds on folly.
All the days of the oppressed are bad, but a cheerful heart has a continual feast.
Better a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure with turmoil.
Better a dish of vegetables where there is love than a fattened ox with hatred.
A hot-tempered man stirs up strife, but he who is slow to anger calms dispute.
The way of the slacker is like a hedge of thorns, but the path of the upright is a highway.
A wise son brings joy to his father, but a foolish man despises his mother.
Folly is joy to one who lacks judgment, but a man of understanding walks a straight path.
Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed.
A man takes joy in a fitting reply— and how good is a timely word!
The path of life leads upward for the wise, that he may avoid going down to Sheol.
The LORD tears down the house of the proud, but He protects the boundaries of the widow.
The LORD detests the thoughts of the wicked, but the words of the pure are pleasant to Him.
He who is greedy for unjust gain brings trouble on his household, but he who hates bribes will live.
The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer, but the mouth of the wicked blurts out evil.
The LORD is far from the wicked, but He hears the prayer of the righteous.
The light of the eyes cheers the heart, and good news nourishes the bones.
He who listens to life-giving reproof will dwell among the wise.
He who ignores discipline despises himself, but whoever heeds correction gains understanding.
The fear of the LORD is the instruction of wisdom, and humility comes before honor.

context.author: Solomon, named in the heading “The proverbs of Solomon” (10:1). The collection runs from 10:1 to 22:16, about 375 sayings.
context.genre: Wisdom sayings: two-line proverbs, most of them contrasts
context.audience: Anyone learning to live wisely, first the young men of Israel’s court and households
context.mapLabel: JERUSALEM, THE ROYAL COURT OF SOLOMON
context.setting: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (v.1). The tongue again holds the center: a soothing tongue is a tree of life (v.4), and a word spoken at the right time is good (v.23). The LORD’s eyes are everywhere, watching the evil and the good (v.3). He detests the sacrifice of the wicked but delights in the prayer of the upright (v.8). Two “better than” sayings show what really counts: a little with the fear of the LORD is better than great treasure with turmoil, and a dish of vegetables with love is better than a fattened ox with hatred (vv.16-17). Plans fail without counsel, but with many advisers they succeed (v.22).
context.custom: Meat was eaten rarely by ordinary families, so a “fattened ox” (v.17) meant a rich feast, while vegetables were the food of the poor. Sacrifices were offered at the Temple, but the prophets and the wise both said that God looks first at the heart of the one who offers (v.8).
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 16 teaches that people make plans but the LORD directs their steps.
context.timelineBible: Samuel told Saul, “obedience is better than sacrifice” (1 Samuel 15:22), and the prophets said the same (Isaiah 1:11-17; Amos 5:21-24). Rehoboam’s refusal to listen to his father’s advisers split the kingdom (1 Kings 12:6-16), the opposite of v.22.

translation.meaning: Soft, tender. A soft answer calms anger.
Confusion, trouble, panic. Riches can bring it.
Advice shared in a circle of friends or advisers.

gospelParallels.note: Slow to speak and slow to anger.
Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt.
Godliness with contentment is great gain (v.16).

otBackground.note: Gideon’s gentle answer calms the men of Ephraim.

overview.summary: A gentle answer turns away anger; the LORD sees all, loves the prayer of the upright, and a little with love is better than plenty with strife.
overview.settingLine: Sayings about the tongue and the heart.

history.t: Sacrifice without a true heart was rejected.

customs.t: Meat was for feasts; greens for every day.

archaeology.t: A horned altar from Beersheba shows how sacrifices were offered.
Clay pots from Iron Age kitchens show a simple daily diet.

overview.discussion: “Better a dish of vegetables where there is love than a fattened ox with hatred” (v.17). Where am I chasing the ox and missing the love?
overview.book: The book of Proverbs · 31 chapters. Short sayings and longer poems that teach how to live wisely in God’s world, beginning with the fear of the LORD.
overview.author: Solomon (10:1)
